extracted.intended_audience: students and readers learning formal/mathematical logic (advanced undergraduates/graduate-level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for (1) expressing properties and relations in first-order theories (definability, axiomatization, expressibility limits) and (2) designing/using derivation systems (sequent calculus, natural deduction, tableaux, axiomatic systems). Intended as textbook criteria and definitions for producing and evaluating formal proofs and theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a given postulate is independent of the other axioms of a theory (e.g., geometry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask if the postulate can be derived from the others or if models exist satisfying the other axioms but not the postulate; independence is a substantive meta-theoretic property of an axiom system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definability of concepts in a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: When a relation or concept of interest can be defined in terms of the primitive symbols of the language (so it need not be added as a primitive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: given ≤ one can define < (and vice versa) by an appropriate formula. The question is: given relations/functions in the language, can another relation R be expressed by a wff α(v1,...,vn) so that |=A α[a1,...,an] iff R(a1,...,an)? If impossible, the relation must be added as a primitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressibility of structural properties by sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Which conditions on a structure A can be expressed by a sentence or set of sentences in the language of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some properties (e.g., reflexivity, antisymmetry, transitivity) have direct first-order sentences. Others (e.g., 'the domain is exactly N' in some languages) cannot be captured by a single sentence. Determine expressibility by constructing appropriate sentences or proving impossibility (using compactness/L¨owenheim–Skolem etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of model of a set of sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A structure A is a model of Γ iff |=A α for all α ∈ Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to evaluate whether a proposed axiom system Γ captures intended structures: check whether intended structures satisfy every axiom and non-intended ones do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatization should capture intended structures (completeness of axiomatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: An axiom system should be chosen so that every intended structure is a model and conversely every model of the axioms is an intended structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: axioms for partial orders (reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive) exactly characterize partial orders; strict linear order axioms similarly. Verify both directions: soundness of axioms for intended models and adequacy (no extraneous models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of axiom schemas / infinite axiom systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Some theories require infinitely many axioms or axiom schemas (e.g., Peano arithmetic uses the induction schema).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about schema form and note that such axiom systems are infinite; document which instances are required and how they function (e.g., induction schema yields infinitely many sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of naive comprehension in set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The naive comprehension principle (for every α(x) ∃y ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ α(x))) is inconsistent (Russell's paradox) and thus unacceptable as an axiom scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use restricted comprehension principles such as separation (∀z ∃y ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ (x ∈ z ∧ α(x)))) as in ZFC. Demonstrate inconsistency of naive comprehension by deriving the Russell sentence ∃y ∀x (x ∈ y ↔ ¬x ∈ x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: when a formula expresses a relation in a structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula α(v1,...,vn) expresses a relation R ⊆ |A|^n iff for all assignments s with s(vi)=ai, |=A α[s] iff R(a1,...,an).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion when claiming that a particular wff defines a relation (e.g., successor, predecessor, ≤) in a model; remember variable assignments mediate between language terms and domain elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing set-theoretic operations and relations within pure set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without function or constant symbols, set operations (subset, union, power set), ordered pairs, products, and functions can be expressed by explicit first-order formulas in the language of ∈.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give explicit defining wffs (e.g., x ⊆ y by ∀z (z ∈ x → z ∈ y); X ∪ Y = Z by ∀u ((u ∈ x ∨ u ∈ y) ↔ u ∈ z); ordered pair ⟨x,y⟩ = z by a formula characterizing {{x},{x,y}}). Note that such definitions do not introduce new term-formation rules; one must substitute entire wffs where needed and ensure axioms assert existence when required (e.g., power set axiom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing cardinality / size properties of structures
rubrics_metrics.description: There are standard sentences that assert 'at least n' (α≥n) or 'exactly n' (α=n) elements in the domain; infinitude can be expressed by an infinite set {α≥1,α≥2,...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the explicit existential formulas given (α≥n and α=n) to assert finite cardinalities. Note limitations: there is no single purely logical sentence that is true in A iff |A| is infinite; moreover, some properties like 'finite' or 'non-enumerable' cannot be captured even by arbitrary sets of sentences due to compactness and L¨owenheim–Skolem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation systems should be mechanically verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation system should make it mechanically checkable whether a given finite syntactic object (sequence/tree) is a correct derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design axioms and inference rules so that each step can be algorithmically checked (this underlies the purpose of derivation systems and motivates choices like sequent calculus, tableaux, or resolution for mechanization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match syntactic derivability with semantic entailment (soundness and completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation system should satisfy: (1) soundness: ⊢ α implies ⊨ α (and Γ ⊢ α implies Γ ⊨ α); (2) completeness: ⊨ α implies ⊢ α (and Γ ⊨ α implies Γ ⊢ α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove soundness for any proposed rules (straightforward) and completeness (often harder). Note some logics have no complete derivation systems; first-order logic does (G¨odel completeness theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency corresponds to satisfiability
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of sentences Γ is syntactically inconsistent (derives every sentence) iff it is unsatisfiable; consistency should coincide with satisfiability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the equivalence between consistency and satisfiability as a design/verification target for derivation systems; the 'consistency implies satisfiability' direction is completeness-like, the converse is soundness-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequent calculus: structure and inference criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequent calculus operates with sequents Γ ⇒ Δ (pairs of sequences of sentences); derivations are trees of sequents where initial sequents/axioms are at the leaves and each sequent follows from premises by explicit inference rules (e.g., ∧L, →R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use/evaluate sequent calculus: check that each rule application manipulates left/right sequences correctly, that initial sequents are of the specified form, and that derivability ⊢ is defined via existence of a derivation with Γ0 ⇒ α where Γ0 ⊆ Γ. Note pros/cons: systematic, symmetric, elegant; derivations can be hard to read though relatively easy to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural deduction: mirroring natural reasoning and discharge of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural deduction provides introduction/elimination rules for connectives and quantifiers, uses assumptions at leaves which may be discharged by rules (e.g., →Intro, ∨Elim), and defines Γ ⊢ α when there is a derivation whose undischarged assumptions are contained in Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess natural deduction proofs by tracking which assumptions are discharged. Favor natural deduction when human-readability and closeness to informal mathematical proof are priorities; use labels/numbers to track discharged assumptions as in textbook style (Fitch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tableaux (truth-tree) method: signed formulas and closure condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Tableaux use signed formulas (T α, F α) on branches; rules expand branches into immediate sub-signed formulas; a tableau is closed if every branch contains a matching T α and F α; Γ ⊢ α iff some finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ yields a closed tableau for {F α, T β1,...,T βn}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tableaux are systematic and particularly amenable to implementation; closed tableaux show unsatisfiability, and open fully-expanded branches can be read to produce satisfying structures. Keep in mind readability of tableaux may be low despite mechanical ease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic derivations: allowed step criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: In an axiomatic (Hilbert-style) system a derivation is a finite sequence α1,...,αn where each αi is either (1) an axiom, (2) a member of Γ, or (3) follows from earlier lines by a rule of inference (e.g., modus ponens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate or construct axiomatic derivations, ensure each line meets one of the three conditions. Axiomatic systems are proof-theoretically simple and suitable for meta-theoretic work but are often hard to use in practice for producing human-readable proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of derivability and theorem (formal criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ⊢ α iff there is a derivation from Γ ending in α. A wff α is a theorem (⊢ α) iff there is a derivation of α from the empty set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these definitions uniformly when comparing derivation systems; they fix what it means to 'prove' syntactically in each formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom schemas for propositional connectives (Ax0)
rubrics_metrics.description: The textbook lists a standard set Ax0 of propositional axiom schemas (examples include (α ∧ β) → α, α → (β → (α ∧ β)), α → (α ∨ β), (α → (β → γ)) → ((α → β) → (α → γ)), (α → β) → ((α → ¬β) → ¬α), ¬¬α → α, ⊤, ⊥ → α, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting an axiomatic system, include explicit axiom schemas as given; each occurrence is an axiom instance. These schemas together with rules (e.g., mp) serve to derive propositional theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens as primary rule of inference (mp)
rubrics_metrics.description: If β and β → α already occur in a derivation, then α is a correct inference step (modus ponens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mp as the core single-step inference rule in many Hilbert-style systems; ensure presence of both premise and implication earlier in the sequence for justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms and rules for quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifier axioms: instances of ∀x β → β(t) and β(t) → ∃x β for any closed term t. Quantifier rules (qr): from β → α(a) with a not occurring in Γ or β infer β → ∀x α(x); from α(a) → β with a not in Γ or β infer ∃x α(x) → β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing axiomatic derivations with quantifiers, apply these axiom instances and qr rules only when side-conditions on the parameter symbol (a) are satisfied (freshness conditions). These ensure correct generalization and instantiation behavior.
